'''George Sinclair''' (Sinclar) ({{circa|1630–1696}})<ref>[https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsnr.2017.0044 Craik, A.D.D., 2018, Royal Society Journal of the History of Science 72(3), he hydrostatical works of George Sinclair (c.1630–1696): their neglect and criticism]</ref><ref name=":0">[https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsnr.2018.0048 Craik, A.D.D. & Spittle, D., 2018, Royal Society Journal of the History of Science 73(1), The hydrostatical works of George Sinclair (c. 1630–1696): an addendum]</ref> was a [[Scottish people|Scottish]] [[mathematician]], [[engineer]] and [[demonologist]]. The first [[Professor of Mathematics (Glasgow)|Professor of Mathematics at the University of Glasgow]], he is known for ''Satan's Invisible World Discovered'', ({{circa|1685}}), a work on [[witchcraft]], ghosts and other supernatural phenomena. He wrote in all three areas of his interests, including an account of the "Glenluce Devil", a [[poltergeist]] case from {{circa|1654}}, in a 1672 book mainly on [[hydrostatics]] but also a pioneering study of geological structures through his experience in [[coal]] [[Mining|mines]].

==Life==
Sinclair was most likely from the [[East Lothian]] area, around [[Haddington, East Lothian|Haddington]]. He studied at the [[University of St Andrews]] between the years 1645 and 1646, but moved to complete his studies at the [[University of Edinburgh]] obtaining a Master of Arts degree from there in 1649.<ref name=":0" />

He became a professor at the [[University of Glasgow]], on 18 April 1654, initially in a [[philosophy]] chair, then moved to a chair founded for mathematics. He helped to fund the building of Glasgow College in 1656.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sinclair |first=George |title=Satan's Invisible World Discovered |date=1871 |publisher=T.G. Stevenson |location=Edinburgh}}</ref> In 1655 he made descents in a [[diving bell]] off the [[Isle of Mull]], to look at the wreck of a ship from the [[Spanish Armada]] there.<ref name="DNB">{{DNB Cite|wstitle=Sinclair, George (d.1696)}}</ref>

Being a Presbyterian, and failing to take the [[Oath of Allegiance (United Kingdom)|oath of allegiance]], he was deprived of his university post in 1666.<ref name="Jackson">Clare Jackson, ''Restoration Scotland'', 1660-1690: royalist politics, religion and ideas (2003), p. 187.</ref> He then worked as a mineral surveyor and engineer, and was employed in particular by [[James Hope of Hopetoun|Sir James Hope]]. He was brought in by the magistrates of Edinburgh, about 1670, to oversee piping of water from [[Comiston]] into the city.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.electricscotland.com/history/other/sinclair_george.htm|title=George Sinclair|website=www.electricscotland.com|access-date=2019-01-26}}</ref>

On 3 March 1691, University of Edinburgh appointed him again to the professorship of mathematics,<ref>{{Cite ODNB|url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-25615|title=Sinclair, George (d. 1696?), natural philosopher|last1=John|first1=Anderson|last2=McConnell|first2=Anita|year=2004|language=en|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/25615|access-date=2019-01-26}}</ref> which had been newly re-funded after a long vacancy.<ref>{{cite web|work=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive|publisher=University of St Andrews|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Glasgow_maths/|title=Mathematics in Glasgow University in 1883|access-date=2024-05-13}}</ref>

Sinclair invented an early example of a [[perpetual motion]] machine based on the principle of the [[siphon]]. He first proposed this in a Latin work on [[pneumatics]] in 1669.<ref>Povey, Thomas. (2015). ''Professor Povey's Perplexing Problems: Pre-University Physics and Maths''. Oneworld Publications. pp. 209-210. {{ISBN|978-1-78074-775-0}}</ref>

==Glenluce Devil==
[[File:SinclairSatansWorld1685.jpg|thumb|Title page of the first edition of ''Satan's Invisible World Discovered'', published in 1685.]]
In his book ''Satan's Invisible World Discovered'' (1685), Sinclair described an alleged [[poltergeist]] incident known as the Devil of Glenluce. Sinclair described the incident as having a "usefulness for refuting atheism."<ref>Henderson, Lizanne. (2009). ''Fantastical Imaginations: The Supernatural in Scottish History and Culture''. John Donald. p. 95</ref>

The incident is described as having taken place at the house of weaver Gilbert Campbell in [[Glenluce]] during October, 1654. A beggar named Alexander Agnew was refused a handout by Campbell.<ref>Lamont-Brown, Raymond. (1994). ''Scottish Witchcraft''. Chambers. pp. 29-30</ref> Agnew had promised to cause the family harm and over the next two years strange phenomena were alleged to have occurred at the house. This included the mysterious cutting of [[Warp and woof|warp thread]], demonic voices, strange whistling noises and stones being thrown.<ref>Seth, Ronald. (1969). ''In the Name of the Devil: Great Scottish Witchcraft Cases''. Jarrolds. pp. 77-78</ref> The poltergeist claims have been dismissed by researchers as a [[hoax]]. Magic historian [[Thomas Frost (writer)|Thomas Frost]] suggested that the phenomena were the result of [[Magic (illusion)|conjuring]] trickery.<ref>[[Thomas Frost (writer)|Frost, Thomas]]. (1876). ''The Lives of the Conjurors''. London: Tinsley Brothers. pp. 108-110.</ref> The story was given to Sinclair by Campbell's son Thomas, a philosophy student from a college in Glasgow who was living at the household. Folklorist [[Andrew Lang]] suggested that Thomas had produced the phenomena fraudulently.<ref>[[Andrew Lang|Lang, Andrew]]. (1893). ''Fairies and Psychical Research''. In [[Robert Kirk (folklorist)|Robert Kirk]]. ''The Secret Commonwealth of Elves, Fauns and Fairies''. London: David Nutt. pp. 55-56. "In this affair a boy called Thomas, a son of the unlucky householder, was clearly the agent. The phenomena were stone-throwing, beating with sticks, levitation of a plate, and a great deal of voices, probably uttered by the aforesaid Thomas."</ref>

Historian [[David Damrosch]] has noted that Alexander Agnew commonly called the "Jock of Broad Scotland" was the first person in Scottish history to publicly deny the existence of God.<ref>[[David Damrosch|Damrosch, David]]. (1999). ''The Longman Anthology of British Literature''. Longman. pp. 754-755</ref> He was hanged at Dumfries for [[blasphemy]] on 21 May 1656.<ref>[[Leonard Levy|Levy, Leonard Williams]]. (1993). ''Blasphemy: Verbal Offense Against the Sacred, From Moses to Salman Rushdie''. University of California Press. p. 167.</ref>

==Geological pioneer==
A long-neglected aspect deriving from Sinclair's work as a mineral surveyor is that the last part of ''Hydrostaticks'' - ''a short History of Coal'' - includes the first published [[Cross section (geology)|geological cross section]] in which he treats the strata in purely geometric terms.<ref>Mike Leeder,(2020), Measures for Measure, pp.16-26: Chapter 2, Beginning of Coallery: George Sinclair, 'Scoto-Lothiani'</ref>

==Controversy==
[[James Gregory (mathematician)|James Gregory]], then a professor at the [[University of St Andrews]], attacked Sinclair in a 1672 pamphlet ''The New and Great Art of Weighing Vanity'', under the name of Patrick Mather or Mathers, [[beadle|archbeadle]] of the [[University of St Andrews]]. Gregory was both a [[Cartesianism|Cartesian]] and an [[Scottish Episcopal Church|Episcopalian]], and self-consciously invoked the [[Hobbes-Wallis controversy]] in aiming at the [[Nonconformist (Protestantism)|non-conformist]] Sinclair.<ref name = Jackson/> The title of Gregory's pamphlet ridiculed Sinclair's 1669 book ''Ars Nova et Magna Gravitatis et Levitatis'' (''The New and Great Art of Heaviness and Lightness''). An appendix to the work, ''Tentamina de motu penduli et projectorum'',<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://archimedes.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/cgi-bin/toc/toc.cgi?page=1373;dir=hutto_dicti_078_en_1795;step=textonly |title=Archimedes Project |access-date=10 April 2009 |archive-date=5 June 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605100653/http://archimedes.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/cgi-bin/toc/toc.cgi?page=1373;dir=hutto_dicti_078_en_1795;step=textonly |url-status=dead }}</ref> was a more important essay on dynamics, regarded by [[D. T. Whiteside]] as a probable source of [[Isaac Newton]]’s theory of [[Inertia|resisted motion]].<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu//full/1970JHA.....1....5W/0000014.000.html|title=1970JHA.....1....5W Page 14|journal=Journal for the History of Astronomy|bibcode=1970JHA.....1....5W|access-date=2019-01-26|last1=Whiteside |first1=D. T. |year=1970 |volume=1 |page=5 |doi=10.1177/002182867000100103 |s2cid=125845242 }}</ref>  Sinclair wrote an answer to Gregory,<ref>''Cacus pulled out of his den by the heels, or the pamphlet entitled, the New and Great Art of Weighing Vanity examined, and found to be a New and Great Act of Vanity.''</ref> but it remained unpublished.

In 1684 he published as his own a work ''Truth's Victory over Error''. It was in fact an English translation by Sinclair of the [[Latin]] [[inaugural dissertation]] given by [[David Dickson (professor)|David Dickson]], who became [[Professor of Divinity, Glasgow]] in 1640, on the occasion in 1650 when he moved to Edinburgh. This was pointed out in short order.<ref>{{DNB Cite|wstitle=Dickson, David (1583?-1663)}}</ref>
